summary: Defines a profile for X.509 certificates used to validate AS paths in BGPsec. Router certificates are issued under the RPKI to routers in an AS. It also covers CRLs and certification requests, and updates RFC 6487.

eli5.summary: Every router gets an ID card to show it may sign for its network. This defines what the cards look like.

questions: what is a bgpsec router certificate
how does rpki issue router certificates
subtitle: The certificate profile that lets a router prove it may sign BGP route advertisements for its AS.

tldr.problem: BGPsec aims to validate the full AS path of a route with strong cryptography, so routers need certificates showing which AS numbers they may sign for.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC profiles X.509 end entity certificates issued under the RPKI to routers. They carry a dedicated Extended Key Usage value and the AS Resources extension, and omit IP Resources and Subject Information Access. It also profiles certification requests and the validation rules.
tldr.outcome: A BGPsec Router Certificate asserts that the holder of the private key may emit secure route advertisements for the AS numbers named in it. The RFC updates RFC 6487.

facts.label: Common name format
facts.value: ROUTER- followed by the 32-bit ASN as eight hexadecimal digits

today: RFC 8209 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 6487. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it is the profile for BGPsec Router Certificates alongside RFC 8205.

sections.title: What a BGPsec Router Certificate Is
sections.content:
This RFC defines a profile of X.509 end entity (EE) certificates, called BGPsec Router Certificates, for certifying AS paths in the BGPsec protocol. The holder of the matching private key is authorized to send secure route advertisements (BGPsec UPDATEs) on behalf of the AS numbers named in the certificate.

A key property of BGPsec is that every AS along the path can verify that the other ASes on the path authorized the advertisement of the route to the next AS. The RFC is a profile of RFC 6487, which is itself a profile of RFC 5280, so it updates RFC 6487. It sets out certificate fields and extensions, the certification request profile, and the Relying Party (RP) validation procedure.
sections.eli5: A router carries a card that says "I may speak for network number so-and-so". Other routers check the card before trusting what it says about routes.

sections.title: Where It Fits in the RPKI
sections.content:
In the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI), IANA issues a CA certificate to each Regional Internet Registry (RIR), the RIR issues one to an Internet Service Provider (ISP), and the ISP's CA also generates CRLs and issues EE certificates for signed objects such as ROAs and manifests. These are all called Resource Certificates and are profiled in RFC 6487.

A BGPsec Router Certificate is another kind of Resource Certificate. It has minimal impact on RPKI CAs: the CA certificate and CRL profiles, and the algorithms used by the issuing CA, stay as they were. The only impact is that CAs must process a profiled certificate request signed with the algorithms in RFC 8208.

Router certificates are used only to verify the signature on the BGPsec certificate request and the signature on a BGPsec UPDATE message. They are not used to process manifests and ROAs, or to verify signatures on certificates or CRLs.
sections.eli5: Think of a chain of trust: a top authority vouches for regional ones, which vouch for network providers, which hand out the router ID cards.

sections.title: Certificate Fields and Extensions
sections.content:
The RFC lists only the differences from the RFC 6487 profile. For the Subject, the common name is encoded as printableString or UTF8String. It is RECOMMENDED to hold the literal string ROUTER- followed by the 32-bit ASN as eight hexadecimal digits, with the serial number attribute holding the 32-bit BGP Identifier (router ID) as eight hexadecimal digits.

The extensions are:

  • Basic Constraints: must not be present, since BGPsec speakers are EEs.
  • Extended Key Usage: MUST be present, not critical, and must include the new id-kp-bgpsec-router value, defined as { id-kp 30 }.
  • Subject Information Access and IP Resources: MUST be omitted.
  • AS Resources: MUST be present with one or more ASNs, and the inherit element MUST NOT be specified.

A BGPsec router MUST require the EKU, and MUST reject certificates lacking the BGPsec Router EKU even if they include anyExtendedKeyUsage.
sections.eli5: The card must say "router" on it, list which networks it speaks for, and must not claim any other powers.

sections.title: Certification Requests
sections.content:
A router asks for its certificate with a request profiled in RFC 6487 Section 6, with a few differences. If the request has Basic Constraints, the CA MUST NOT honor a cA boolean set to TRUE. If it has the EKU extension, id-kp-bgpsec-router MUST be present and the CA MUST honor it. If it asks for Subject Information Access, the CA MUST NOT honor that. The public key format and the signature algorithms come from RFC 8208.

The design notes explain that the CA must issue a properly formed certificate regardless of what the request contains, as required by the RPKI Certificate Policy. So a request for a CA certificate yields an EE certificate, a request for keyCertSign or cRLSign yields a certificate with neither, a request without the BGPsec EKU yields one with it, and a request with an SIA extension yields one without it. This is similar to the CA adding the AS Resources extension even though it is not in the request.
sections.eli5: Even if you scribble extra powers on your ID card application, the office only prints the right kind of card.

sections.title: Validation by Relying Parties
sections.content:
Validation follows the RFC 6487 Section 7 procedure, with these differences: the certificate MUST include the BGPsec Router EKU, MUST NOT include SIA or IP Resources, MUST include AS Resources, and MUST include the subjectPublicKeyInfo field described in RFC 8208. The step requiring all mandatory fields refers to the fields this RFC requires.

BGPsec RPs need to support the algorithms in RFC 8208 to validate BGPsec signatures, and the algorithms in RFC 7935 to validate signatures on BGPsec certificates, RPKI CA certificates and RPKI CRLs.

The private key of a router EE certificate may be used many times, in many Signature Segments of the BGPsec_PATH attribute. Certificates are stored in the issuing CA's repository, where a repository following RFC 6481 MUST use a .cer filename extension.
sections.eli5: The checker follows the usual ID-check steps but also makes sure the card has the "router" stamp and no forbidden extras.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
A certificate may list several ASNs. In that case it becomes invalid if any one of them is removed from any superior CA certificate along the path to a trust anchor. Operators could avoid this by issuing a separate BGPsec Router Certificate for each ASN, so that the certificates for the retained ASNs stay valid.

If the same certificate is issued to more than one router, the private key is shared among them, and the issuer chooses which router ID appears in the name.
sections.eli5: If one card lists many networks and one of them is taken away, the whole card is voided. Separate cards avoid that.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 6487 apply. A BGPsec Router Certificate fails ordinary RPKI validation because the cryptographic algorithms differ, so an RP must look at the EKU to pick the right validation constraints.

The certificate's essential security function is the secure binding of one or more ASNs to a public key, consistent with the RPKI allocation hierarchy. Hash functions are used for the Subject Key Identifier and Issuer Key Identifier. Collision resistance is not required for key identifiers, per RFC 6818, and collisions are unlikely but possible. A Subject Key Identifier collision might cause the wrong certificate to be selected from the cache and a failed signature validation, and the operator should be alerted if one is detected.
sections.eli5: The card ties a network number to a secret key. If two cards looked alike by accident, a checker could pick the wrong one, so people should be told when that happens.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC uses two object identifiers in the SMI registry for PKIX. One identifies the ASN.1 module in Appendix A, id-mod-bgpsec-eku, from the "SMI Security for PKIX Module Identifier" registry. The other is the BGPsec Router EKU, id-kp-bgpsec-router, from the "SMI Security for PKIX Extended Key Purpose" registry.

These OIDs were assigned before management of the PKIX arc was handed to IANA, and the registry references were updated to point to this document.
sections.eli5: The special "router" stamp has an official number in a registry, so everyone uses the same stamp.
